/-!
# Wieferich primes in base 47

A *Wieferich prime in base $a$* is a prime $p$ such that $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$.
The classical Wieferich primes are those in base $2$; the only known ones are $1093$ and $3511$.
Base $47$ is the smallest base $a > 1$ for which no Wieferich prime is known.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [Wikipedia, Wieferich prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wieferich_prime)
* [OEIS A039951](https://oeis.org/A039951)
-/

$p^2 \mid 47^{p-1} - 1$?

The usual proviso $p \nmid 47$ is omitted because it is automatic: the prime $p = 47$ does not
satisfy the divisibility condition.

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no question, the Prop being ∃ prime p with p^2 ∣ 47^(p−1) − 1; the usual coprimality proviso p ∤ a is vacuous here since p = 47 (and p = 2) automatically fail the congruence, so the base-47 Wieferich condition needs no extra hypothesis, and the article's generalized-Wieferich material (base 47 being the smallest base with no known example) only makes the terse list entry precise rather than adding further questions.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same faithful Prop `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ (p^2 ∣ 47^(p-1) - 1  or  47^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2])`; the two forms are equivalent for prime p (p ≥ 2 so 47^(p-1) ≥ 47 and ℕ-subtraction does not truncate). I took c05's file: divisibility form literally matching the decomposition note, inline statement (no bespoke definition needed for a single fixed base — c04's generic `IsWieferichPrime` would belong in FormalConjecturesForMathlib, not a problem file), plus two `@[category test]` lemmas (`norm_num`-proved) recording that p = 47 and p = 2 fail the condition, which documents why the usual `p ∤ a` proviso is dropped. Docstring lightly tightened. Verified in Lean: no prime p < 20000 is a base-47 witness (so neither `p ∤ 47` nor the article's `1 < a < p` table convention changes the predicate), the same formula in base 2 picks out exactly 1093 and 3511, and `answer(sorry)` scopes as `(answer) ↔ (∃ …)` with `answer(True)` = witnesses exist, `answer(False)` = none. Compiles with only the `declaration uses 'sorry'` warning.

context:
In number theory, a Wieferich prime is a prime number p such that p2 divides 2p − 1 − 1, therefore connecting these primes with Fermat's little theorem, which states that every odd prime p divides 2p − 1 − 1. Wieferich primes were first described by Arthur Wieferich in 1909 in works pertaining to Fermat's Last Theorem, at which time both of Fermat's theorems were already well known to mathematicians.
Since then, connections between Wieferich primes and various other topics in mathematics have been discovered, including other types of numbers and primes, such as Mersenne and Fermat numbers, specific types of pseudoprimes and some types of numbers generalized from the original definition of a Wieferich prime. Over time, those connections discovered have extended to cover more properties of certain prime numbers as well as more general subjects such as number fields and the abc conjecture.
As of 2026, the only known Wieferich primes are 1093 and 3511 (sequence A001220 in the OEIS).

decomposition_objections.text: None. The single-slot decomposition is correct: the entry is one yes/no question, and the note that the p ∤ 47 proviso is vacuous (p = 2 and p = 47 both fail the congruence) is accurate and was machine-checked in the file's test lemmas.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Wieferich primes in base 47

A *Wieferich prime in base $a$* is a prime $p$ such that $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$.
The classical Wieferich primes are those in base $2$; the only known ones are $1093$ and $3511$.
Base $47$ is the smallest base $a > 1$ for which no Wieferich prime is known.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [Wikipedia, Wieferich prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wieferich_prime)
* [OEIS A039951](https://oeis.org/A039951)
-/

namespace WieferichPrime

/--
Are there any Wieferich primes in base $47$? That is, does there exist a prime $p$ such that
$p^2 \mid 47^{p-1} - 1$?

The usual proviso $p \nmid 47$ is omitted because it is automatic: the prime $p = 47$ does not
satisfy the divisibility condition.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem wieferich_prime : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ p ^ 2 ∣ 47 ^ (p - 1) - 1 := by
  sorry

/-- The prime $47$ is not a Wieferich prime in base $47$, so no coprimality hypothesis is needed
in `wieferich_prime`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_dvd_of_eq_47 : ¬ 47 ^ 2 ∣ 47 ^ (47 - 1) - 1 := by
  norm_num

/-- The prime $2$ is not a Wieferich prime in base $47$: $47^1 - 1 = 46$ is not divisible by
$4$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_dvd_of_eq_two : ¬ 2 ^ 2 ∣ 47 ^ (2 - 1) - 1 := by
  norm_num

end WieferichPrime

items: The list entry is terse; the precise reading used is the standard one from the article's generalized-Wieferich material: a Wieferich prime in base a is a prime p (with p ∤ a) such that p² ∣ a^(p−1) − 1. For a = 47 this gives `∃ p, p.Prime ∧ p ^ 2 ∣ 47 ^ (p - 1) - 1`.

The coprimality proviso p ∤ 47 is omitted because it is vacuous: p = 47 fails the congruence (47^46 ≡ −1 mod 47), and p = 2 fails too (4 ∤ 46). Both facts are recorded as `@[category test]` lemmas proved by `norm_num`, so the statement without the proviso is exactly the base-47 Wieferich question.
The question is formalized in the repository's preferred `answer(sorry) ↔ P` style for yes/no questions; `answer(True)` asserts a base-47 Wieferich prime exists, `answer(False)` asserts none does.

Arithmetic is in ℕ with truncated subtraction; this is harmless since for prime p one has p − 1 ≥ 1 and 47^(p−1) ≥ 47 > 1, so `47 ^ (p - 1) - 1` equals the integer value. Divisibility `p ^ 2 ∣ 47 ^ (p - 1) - 1` was chosen over `Nat.ModEq` to match the decomposition note literally; the two are equivalent.

No bespoke definition was introduced (Mathlib and FormalConjecturesForMathlib have no Wieferich-prime notion; only Wall–Sun–Sun/Lucas–Wieferich exist in FormalConjecturesForMathlib, which are different objects). The single-base condition is short enough to state inline, following the decomposition's explicit Prop.

The module docstring's claim that 47 is the smallest base with no known Wieferich prime comes from the article's base-a table (and OEIS A039951); the sandbox snapshot of the article omits that table section, so a reviewer may wish to confirm against the live article.

reviewer_notes: Statement is a terse list entry; the precise notion ('Wieferich prime in base a': prime p with a^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p^2) comes from the Wieferich prime article, whose relevant section is truncated in the sandbox snapshot but is standard (OEIS A039951, a(47) unknown). The decomposition's claim that the coprimality proviso is vacuous was machine-checked (47^46 ≡ 0 mod 47^2, 4 ∤ 46) and, more strongly, no prime below 20000 satisfies the base-47 congruence, so the alternative 'a < p' reading is also immaterial. No candidate omitted the slot; no objections to the decomposition were raised, and I concur. Candidates differ only cosmetically (ModEq vs dvd, bespoke def in c04, test lemmas in c04/c05). The module docstring's claim that 47 is the smallest base with no known Wieferich prime is consistent with OEIS A039951 (values known for all 2 ≤ n ≤ 46).
